Battle of Chickamauga. From September eighteenth to twentieth, eighteen sixty-three, the second-bloodiest battle of the American Civil War unfolded in northwestern Georgia near the Tennessee border. Union General William S. Rosecrans had maneuvered Confederate General Braxton Bragg into a retreat, but Bragg rallied his forces and, reinforced by divisions detached from other theaters, caught Rosecrans overextended. What followed was a two-day battle of fierce combat that broke the Union right. Only the steadfast defense of Union General George H. Thomas at the end of September nineteenth prevented complete rout. Though Confederates held the field, their failure to capitalize on Rosecrans' rout and their own heavy casualties prevented a decisive victory.

Rosecrans sought to maneuver Bragg out of middle Tennessee without direct engagement. Bragg initially retreated but, learning that Union supply lines were extended and the army dispersed, resolved to attack. Confederate reinforcements, including James Longstreet's corps from the Virginia theater, arrived to strengthen Bragg's position.

Initial skirmishing on September eighteenth escalated into frontal attacks on September nineteenth and twentieth. The Union right, commanded by General Alexander McCook, broke under Confederate assault, creating a rout that Rosecrans followed in retreat to Chattanooga. But General George H. Thomas, with a small reserve force, held Horseshoe Ridge on the evening of September nineteenth and all through September twentieth, earning the epithet "Rock of Chickamauga." His stand prevented annihilation of the army.

Bragg did not pursue Rosecrans after the Union withdrawal. The Union was besieged in Chattanooga but not destroyed. Casualties were approximately eighteen thousand on each side—a heavy toll that benefited neither side strategically.

Chickamauga was a pyrrhic Confederate victory. Bragg had briefly restored Confederate fortunes in the western theater, but his failure to destroy or capture Rosecrans' army and his subsequent passivity allowed the Union to consolidate. The arrival of reinforcements from Virginia showed the Confederacy's ability to concentrate force when necessary, yet the detachment weakened Lee elsewhere. Thomas's heroic stand exemplified individual courage's power to alter a battle's trajectory, yet courage alone could not overcome Union industrial advantage. The siege of Chattanooga that followed would become another turning point when Union forces under Ulysses S. Grant broke through.
